Color vocabulary

Explore the terms, relationships, and practical ideas behind color in design.

Color properties

Hue

The basic color family, such as red, green, or blue.

Saturation

The intensity of a color. Higher saturation generally appears vivid; lower saturation appears muted or grayish.

Value

How light or dark a color appears. Higher values are lighter; lower values are darker.

Tint

Traditionally, a color mixed with white.

Shade

Traditionally, a color mixed with black.

Tone

Traditionally, a color mixed with gray. Digital tools may use tint, shade, and tone differently.

Color temperature

A way to describe colors as relatively warm or cool. A warm off-white may feel more inviting than a cooler one.

Color scale

A sequence of related color variations, often used to support different roles and states.

Brightness and lightness

Related ways to describe perceived intensity and lightness, but they are not always technically identical.

Palettes and relationships

Color palette

A collection of colors chosen to work together. A color wheel can help explore combinations.

Color relationships

How colors interact visually. For example, warm colors can balance cooler colors.

Color harmony

A way of describing how colors relate visually and work together. A color wheel can help, but harmony also depends on context and judgment.

Complementary colors

Two hues opposite each other on a color wheel, such as blue and orange on a traditional wheel. They can create strong visual contrast.

Analogous colors

Hues next to each other on a color wheel, such as blue, cyan, and green. They can feel unified, but similar saturation and value can make hierarchy harder to establish.

Triadic colors

Three hues spaced approximately equally around a color wheel. They can create variety and energy, but giving each equal visual weight may feel busy.

Split-complementary colors

A base hue and the two hues on either side of its complement. For example, a traditional wheel can pair blue with yellow-orange and red-orange.

Square color harmony

Four hues spaced approximately equally around a color wheel. They offer variety and more opportunities for colors to compete. A palette does not require every hue in every component.

Palette size

How many distinct colors are available. More colors can be intentional and expressive; the goal is to avoid unnecessary complexity.

Palette efficiency

How effectively a palette provides the needed variety. A few foundational hues can produce many variations through tints, shades, and tones.

Palette distribution

How much space and attention each color receives. A primary brand color does not need to dominate every component.

60-30-10 rule

A heuristic for distributing dominant, secondary, and accent colors. It is not an accessibility standard or a mathematical requirement, and proportions alone do not establish hierarchy.

Color placement

Where a color appears. Placement can affect what people notice as much as the amount of color used.

Prominence

How much an element stands out in relation to its surroundings.

Color vibration

A visually unstable or uncomfortable effect that can occur when highly saturated colors with similar perceived brightness sit next to each other. Check measurable text contrast and visual comfort separately.

Interface color roles

Accent color

A supporting color used selectively to highlight elements or add variety. It does not have to be complementary to the primary color.

Supporting colors

Colors used alongside a primary color to provide balance, hierarchy, or variety.

Neutral colors

Colors such as white, black, gray, and near-neutral variations. They influence an interface’s atmosphere even when they receive little attention.

Semantic color

A color used to communicate a purpose or meaning in an interface, such as an error state.

Semantic color system

A system that assigns colors responsibilities instead of choosing them solely for appearance. Do not rely on color alone to communicate meaning.

Visual hierarchy

The arrangement of elements that helps people understand their relative importance. Color is one of several tools for establishing hierarchy.

Brand identity

The recognizable qualities of a brand. Existing and new colors should support or deliberately evolve that identity.

Design consistency

Applying choices predictably according to their roles. Consistency does not require every component to use the same color.

Visual cue

A signal that helps someone identify, interpret, or use an element, such as a label, icon, shape, or placement.

Coverage

How much space a color occupies.

Frequency

How often a color appears. Repetition can influence its perceived importance.

Interactive state

A condition of a control, such as default, hover, focus, pressed, or disabled.

Hover

A state that can indicate pointer interaction. Touch users may not have a hover state.

Focus

The state identifying the element ready to receive input, often shown with a visible focus indicator.

Iterative design

A process of reviewing, testing, and refining a design. Changing one variable at a time can help isolate its effect.

Design systems and tokens

Design system

A shared collection of principles, components, and guidance that helps a team create consistent experiences, including rules for color.

Design token

A reusable, named design decision, such as a color or spacing value. A small set of foundational colors can support many variations and roles.

Color token

A design token that represents a color value or a color’s purpose.

Primitive token

A named foundational value, such as pink-500: #EC4899.

Semantic token

A named purpose that references a value, such as action-primary-background referencing pink-500. This separates the purpose from the underlying color.

Paired semantic tokens

Related role tokens used together, such as a background and the text displayed on it. Check the contrast of the actual pair.

Contextual semantic token

A role token that also identifies the context in which it is used, such as text on a dark surface.

Component token

A token for a specific component, such as button-primary-background. It can provide customization but adds complexity; more layers are not automatically better.

Component variant

A named version of a component that serves a distinct purpose, such as a featured button. Its styles can reference semantic tokens.

Semantic variant and contextual override

A semantic variant describes why a component differs; a contextual override describes where a difference applies.

Token reference

A connection between tokens or between a token and a component. Following references helps determine which elements change when a color is updated.

Accessibility and evaluation

Contrast

The visual difference between elements, such as text and its background, that helps distinguish them.

Contrast ratio

A measurement of the difference in relative luminance between two colors.

Text contrast

WCAG AA generally requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Large text is at least 18pt regular or 14pt bold; exceptions apply.

Readability

How easy text is to read. Contrast, typography, size, spacing, and layout all contribute. Passing a contrast check alone does not guarantee readability.

Visual comfort

Whether a combination feels stable and comfortable to look at. Evaluate it alongside measurable contrast.

User research

Ways to learn about users and their needs, including observing people and gathering feedback. Analytics can help identify potential problems.

User goals

What visitors are trying to accomplish. Compare observed behavior with those goals before interpreting results.

Problem identification

Define what needs to improve before choosing a solution, such as changing a palette.

Psychology and interpretation

Color psychology

The study and discussion of how people perceive and respond to colors, including possible emotional associations.

Color association

An idea or feeling a color may bring to mind. Red, for example, can suggest urgency or passion.

Color interpretation

The meaning someone takes from a color in context. A vivid red can suggest energy, burgundy elegance, and a light red softness; interpretations vary.

Common color associations

These are possible associations, not universal meanings. Culture, experience, saturation, lightness, and surrounding colors can change interpretation.

ColorPossible associations
RedDanger, urgency, passion, love
OrangeEnergy, warmth, enthusiasm
YellowOptimism, happiness, caution
GreenNature, growth, health, success
BlueTrust, calmness, reliability
PurpleCreativity, luxury, spirituality
PinkRomance, sensitivity, playfulness
BlackPower, sophistication, elegance
WhiteSimplicity, cleanliness, purity
GrayNeutrality, professionalism, restraint
